strengths: L4Q addresses a relevant NLP deployment problem: combining parameter-efficient adaptation with quantization while eliminating the separate high-precision LoRA branch at inference. Quantizing the merged base weights and low-rank update is a coherent design.

The evaluation covers seven model configurations spanning 3B–33B parameters, two bit widths, commonsense tasks, and MMLU. Some improvements are substantial: at 3 bits, LLaMA-2 7B achieves 61.3 CSQA accuracy versus 57.4 for QAT-LoRA and 57.6 for QLoRA*.

The reported efficiency results are promising. For 7B training, L4Q uses 25.4 GB versus 79.5 GB for full QAT and 25.1 GB for LoRA. Appendix F also provides useful evidence that removing the adapter branch improves inference throughput under a shared quantization kernel.

The QAT-LoRA comparison and ablations of initialization, rank, and group size help explain design choices. The forward computation and distinction between merged and unmerged inference are presented clearly.
weaknesses: Reproducibility remains insufficiently established for the central efficiency claims. Although several hyperparameters are supplied, the manuscript lacks an implementation link or complete backward pseudocode and omits microbatch size, gradient accumulation, activation checkpointing, and the LoRA scaling value. Appendix D's 25K/50K iterations with batch size 128 also need reconciliation with the one-epoch convergence plot and the distinction between iterations and optimizer steps.

Training-cost comparisons are confounded. Appendix D uses sequence length 128 only for L4Q on the 33B model, versus 2048 otherwise, materially affecting memory, computation, and training content. Different training durations are justified mainly through training loss on one model, without a documented validation-based selection procedure. Matched workloads and time-to-comparable-quality measurements are needed. L4Q also retains substantially higher training memory than QLoRA: 25.4 versus 7.9 GB at 7B.

Baseline validation limits the superiority claim. Replacing QLoRA's and LoftQ's native quantization with uniform quantization is understandable for kernel-controlled comparisons, but changes those methods. LoftQ* frequently collapses to near-chance 3-bit MMLU performance, yet its training and initialization settings are not adequately documented or diagnosed. These results support comparisons with the specified variants more directly than with the original methods.

The backward equations need correction or clarification. With G = dL/dWq and the elementwise clipping mask M, the STE gradients should be dL/dA = αBᵀ(G ⊙ M) and dL/dB = α(G ⊙ M)Aᵀ. Equations 29–30 place a matrix-valued condition outside these contractions, leaving mixed clipped/unclipped cases ill-defined. This does not establish an implementation error, but matters because the custom backward is central to the contribution.

The mechanistic explanation overstates the distinction from QAT-LoRA. Its quantization and adapter parameters already influence a shared loss; separate computational branches do not imply independent optimization. Likewise, temporary weight gradients need not inherently remain stored across layers. Controlled ablations using identical initialization and memory handling would better isolate the benefits of quantization placement.

Many improvements over the strongest baseline are only 0.1–0.3 percentage points, with no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. Superiority is also not universal: 3-bit LLaMA-2 13B MMLU 5-shot is 50.0 versus QLoRA*'s 50.6. Combined with training on one English instruction dataset and exclusively multiple-choice evaluation, this warrants narrower claims. The promising results make Findings plausible, but the unresolved implementation and comparison issues prevent a clear positive recommendation.
